rules: A pattern is a method. It may suggest a structure; it never states a fact about an organisation.
Every element a pattern suggests still needs the organisation's own evidence. Without it, the element is an assumption, with what breaks if it is false.
A pattern never raises the label of a statement, never closes an unknown and never settles a contradiction.
A pattern names role-types only: never a person or a position.
This catalogue holds no organisation's data and no copied text. Each pattern is a plain description of a widely known way to organise.

patterns.name: Functional organisation
patterns.summary: Work is grouped by kind of expertise, such as sales, operations, finance and people. Each function has one accountable lead, and the top role joins the functions together.
typical_capabilities: Direction and governance
Sales and customer relations
Operations or delivery
Finance
People
Support services, such as legal, premises and information

decision_rights.decision: Overall direction and priorities
The budget across functions
decision_rights.role_type: the top role, advised by the finance lead

decision_rights.decision: Methods and standards inside a function
Hiring inside an approved budget

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: a confirmed order or commitment to deliver
delivery records for billing
spending requests inside the budget
newly filled positions ready to work

fits_when: There is one main line of products or services.
The organisation serves one market or a few similar ones.
Depth of expertise matters more than speed across functions.
does_not_fit_when: There are several distinct product lines or markets that need their own priorities.
Most work needs fast coordination across many functions every day.
known_risks: Each function serves its own goals before the whole.
Decisions that cross functions are slow and pile up at the top role.
No one owns a customer's whole experience.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Divisional organisation
patterns.summary: The organisation is split into divisions by product, market, customer group or region. Each division holds most of the functions it needs and answers for its own results, under a small centre.
typical_capabilities: Direction of the whole and allocation of capital, at the centre
Rules for the whole, such as financial reporting, risk and legal, set at the centre
In each division: its sales, its delivery and its management
Review of each division's results

decision_rights.decision: The strategy of the whole, and capital between divisions
decision_rights.role_type: the top role at the centre

decision_rights.decision: A division's plan and operations, inside its targets
Policies that bind every division, such as finance, risk and legal
Prices and offers inside a division

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: targets, capital and the policies that bind it
results and forecasts
shared customers or internal supply, on agreed terms

fits_when: Products, markets or regions differ enough to need their own priorities.
Each division is large enough to carry its own functions.
Results can be measured division by division.
does_not_fit_when: The organisation is too small to repeat functions in each division.
The products share most of their customers and their ways of working.
known_risks: Functions are repeated in every division, at a cost.
Divisions compete for customers or resources.
The centre loses sight of risks that cross divisions.
Practices drift apart between divisions.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Matrix organisation
patterns.summary: Two lines of accountability cross: one by function or expertise, one by product, project, market or region. Many roles answer to both, so the decision rights must say which line decides what.
typical_capabilities: Function leadership: standards, expertise and people
Product, project or market leadership: priorities and results
Joint planning of the time of positions shared by the two lines
Settling conflicts between the two lines

decision_rights.decision: What is delivered, and when
decision_rights.role_type: the product, project or market lead

decision_rights.decision: How the work is done, and its quality standards
How the time of shared positions is split
decision_rights.role_type: the two leads jointly, under a rule agreed in advance

decision_rights.decision: A conflict the two lines cannot settle
decision_rights.role_type: a named role above both lines

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: positions and expertise assigned
demand and priorities
conflicts they could not settle

fits_when: The work needs both deep expertise and a strong focus on products, projects or markets.
Scarce experts must be shared.
The organisation can afford the effort of coordination.
does_not_fit_when: The decision rights of the two lines cannot be written down clearly.
The organisation is small, and a second line adds effort without benefit.
known_risks: Accountability becomes unclear.
Decisions slow down, and the two lines come into conflict.
Coordination takes a large share of everyone's time.
People are caught between two leads.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Shared-service centre
patterns.summary: Common support work, such as finance processing, people administration, purchasing or information services, is done once, in one centre, for several units, under agreed service terms.
typical_capabilities: Delivery of the shared services to the units served
Service terms and demand
Reporting on service against its terms
Improvement of the shared ways of working

decision_rights.decision: Which services are shared, and their scope
decision_rights.role_type: the role with authority over all the units served, or, between independent entities, their agreement

decision_rights.decision: Service terms: levels, charges and priorities
decision_rights.role_type: the centre lead and the units served, agreed under that authority

decision_rights.decision: How a service is delivered
Whether a unit may leave a shared service
decision_rights.role_type: the same authority that decided the service is shared

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: requests, and the information the service needs
the completed service and its records
service results against the agreed terms

fits_when: Several units need the same support work, and most of it is standard.
Gains in scale or consistency are worth the extra hand-offs.
Service terms can be stated and checked.
does_not_fit_when: The support work differs a great deal between units, or must sit close to each unit's daily work.
Too few units share the work to gain from scale.
known_risks: The centre drifts away from the units' needs.
Disputes arise over service terms and charges.
Units build their own hidden copies of the service.
One failure in the centre reaches every unit at once.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Holding with independent subsidiaries
patterns.summary: A parent owns several subsidiaries. Each runs as an independent entity, with its own management and its own governing body. The parent acts as owner, not as operator.
typical_capabilities: Ownership and allocation of capital, at the parent
Appointing and overseeing each subsidiary's governing body, as owner
Reporting and accounts for the whole group
In each subsidiary: its own complete operating model

decision_rights.decision: Buying, selling or funding a subsidiary
Appointing a subsidiary's governing body
decision_rights.role_type: the parent, as owner, through the subsidiary's own rules

decision_rights.decision: A subsidiary's strategy and operations
decision_rights.role_type: that subsidiary's own governing body and management

decision_rights.decision: Reporting rules for the whole group
decision_rights.role_type: the parent, within what the law and each subsidiary's own rules allow

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: results and the reports owed to the owner
capital and owner decisions, through the subsidiary's own governing body
dealings on agreed terms, as between independent parties

fits_when: The businesses differ enough to need their own management.
Legal, regulatory or risk separation between them is needed.
The owner wants to be able to buy or sell a business as a whole.
does_not_fit_when: The businesses depend on each other every day and need shared operations.
The parent wants to direct operations itself.
known_risks: The parent directs operations informally and blurs the separation.
Costs are repeated in each subsidiary.
The owner's oversight of each subsidiary's risks is weak.
Dealings between subsidiaries drift away from agreed terms.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Platform with business units
patterns.summary: A central platform provides common capabilities, such as customer access, technology, data, payments or brand, and several business units build their own offers on it. The units own their markets and results; the platform owns the shared capabilities.
typical_capabilities: The platform's capabilities, offered to the units
The platform's plan and priorities
In each unit: its offer, its customers and its results
Rules for using the platform: access, standards and charges

decision_rights.decision: What the platform offers, and in what order
decision_rights.role_type: the platform lead, after hearing the units' demand under an agreed rule

decision_rights.decision: A unit's offer and market
The standards a unit must meet to use the platform
A dispute over the platform's priorities
decision_rights.role_type: a named role with authority over both, or, between independent entities, their agreement

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: a platform capability ready to use
demand, feedback and use
charges or contributions, where agreed

fits_when: Several units need the same core capabilities and gain from sharing them.
The units serve different markets.
The shared capability would be costly to build twice.
does_not_fit_when: The units need very different underlying capabilities.
The platform cannot be run as a service to the units.
Using the platform would turn the units into internal functions of the platform, against their own autonomy.
known_risks: The platform becomes a bottleneck.
The units lose their autonomy to the platform's priorities.
Charges for the platform are unclear.
One failure of the platform stops every unit.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.

patterns.name: Single-position practice
patterns.summary: One position, the practitioner, does or directs all the work, with clients, suppliers, advisers and authorities at the boundary. The roles are hats the one position wears, so the model names each role-type that position carries and what each decides.
typical_capabilities: Finding and agreeing work with clients
Doing the work
Administration and finance
Keeping skills and permissions current
Managing outside suppliers and advisers

decision_rights.decision: Which work to accept, and on what terms
How the work is done
Prices and spending
What is passed to outside suppliers and advisers

typical_hand_offs.what_crosses: a request and the information needed
the delivered work and the invoice
a defined task
the filings and reports owed

fits_when: The work is one practitioner's, with occasional outside help.
A few client relationships or one profession define the work.
does_not_fit_when: The work needs several roles carried by different positions at the same time.
Others hold decision rights over the work.
known_risks: Nobody covers when the practitioner is away.
One position holds every decision, so conflicts between the roles go unseen.
Outside dependencies are not written down.
patterns.never_evidence: This pattern is never evidence for an organisation.
